name: Marco Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Marco. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Kenyon Motors on the ring road, eight bays, busy from the minute the shutters go up. I do a bit of everything, but I'm the one who set up our AI booking system, and I run the diagnostic assistant on most jobs. Phil Kenyon, the owner, calls me the computer kid, though I'm happiest with my arms in an engine bay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like turning a job round fast and right, and the AI helps with that, it finds a maker's technical bulletin in ten seconds that used to take me half an hour. What wears me out is customers who haggle over labour and then leave a one-star review. On the side I buy cars at auction, fix them up in my friend's unit and sell them, about four a year.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ruth, she's a dental hygienist, and I'm proposing at Christmas, though she doesn't know that yet. I've got about nine months of wages saved, plus two project cars and my van. Sundays it's church with Ruth's family, Saturdays I coach the under-twelves football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's a good tool, same as a decent scan tool was twenty years ago, and the hype was overdone. At work I'd tell Phil we got our money's worth from the booking system anyway. Online I'd just keep posting my car flips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a fine world for me. I'm well paid, there are garages all over the city wanting experienced people, and my car flipping keeps growing. The only thing I'd miss is the chance to build something bigger on the back of the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go from four flips a year to eight, and rent my own small unit instead of borrowing my friend's. I'd keep using the AI for the tedious bits, the bulletins and the write-ups. And I'd start putting money aside to buy into Kenyon Motors when Phil retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Renting a unit is a commitment. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the flips. Each one clears me a decent profit after parts, and a small unit costs less a month than one flip makes. I've done the sums on the back of an auction catalogue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy into Kenyon Motors rather than open your own place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Phil's got twenty-five years of customers and a name people trust. I'd rather buy a garage that already works and make it better than fight for every job from scratch.

say: AI's a **good tool**, like scan tools twenty years ago, and the hype was overdone.
The **booking system** still paid for itself at Kenyon Motors.
think: It's a **fine world** for him, with good pay and garages hiring across the city.
He'd miss the chance to **build something bigger** on the back of the tools.
do: Double his **car flips** from four to eight a year.
Rent his **own small unit** instead of borrowing a friend's.
Save toward **buying into** Kenyon Motors when Phil retires.
S0.quote: I'd rather buy a garage that already works and make it better than fight for every job from scratch.
fieldNote: He's an adaptive **free-marketeer** who sees AI as a way to build a business.
His side trade of **auction car flips** is already a real second income.
He prefers **buying an existing business** to starting from nothing.

steps.text: Flip eight auction cars a year instead of four
Rent a small unit of his own for the flips
Save toward buying a share of Kenyon Motors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that one I'd do well out of, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, not a threat, if you're willing to learn. At work I'd be telling the other mechanics to use the diagnostic assistant on every job, not just the hard ones. Online I'd post how much faster we turn cars round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it splits garages in two. The ones that use the tools win the work, and the ones that don't, like the old place round the corner, slowly lose it. The thinking jobs in the office shrink, parts ordering and quotes, but someone who can fix cars and run the systems becomes worth more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd offer Phil a deal: I set up AI quoting and parts ordering across the garage, and he gives me a stake in return. I'd keep flipping cars and use AI to price them at auction. And I'd take on an apprentice myself, because the trade still needs young people learning properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty excited actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the office jobs shrinking. Who at Kenyon Motors does those now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev on reception, she's been there fifteen years. In this picture I'd want Phil to move her onto customer care, the human side, rather than let her go. People still want someone to explain the bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why take on an apprentice yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how I learned, from an old mechanic called Tony who made me do everything twice. Government schemes are fine, but the trade's passed on by people. If AI does the garage paperwork, there's more time for teaching apprentices.

say: This is **a chance**, not a threat, for anyone willing to learn.
Mechanics should use the **diagnostic assistant** on every job.
think: Garages will **split in two**, with those using the tools winning the work.
A mechanic who **runs the systems** becomes worth more as office jobs shrink.
do: Offer Phil AI quoting and ordering in exchange for **a stake** in the garage.
Use AI to **price auction cars** for his flips.
Take on an **apprentice** of his own.
S1.quote: If AI does the garage paperwork, there's more time for teaching apprentices.
fieldNote: He treats the change as a **business opportunity** and trades skills for ownership.
He wants Bev on reception moved to **customer care**, not let go.
His belief in **apprenticeships** is personal, rooted in his old mentor Tony.

steps.text: Set up AI quoting and parts ordering across Kenyon Motors
Trade that setup work for a stake in the garage
Use AI price checks when buying auction cars to flip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. That's where it gets real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say mechanics have a few years' head start because the robots come later, so use them. I'd tell the parents at football to think hard about what their kids study. I wouldn't panic online, I'd post what I'm doing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my diagnosis skill is worth a lot less in 2028, because the AI does it better. Then in 2031 the robots come for the spanner work, when I'm 32. The only safe place is owning the business that owns the robots, not being the man they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd go to Phil and offer to buy a share of Kenyon Motors with my savings and the project cars. I'd push the garage to be first in the city with the new AI systems, so we're the ones taking the work. I'd still propose at Christmas, but with a cheaper ring, and the rest goes into the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more fired up than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Phil says no to selling you a share?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look at the old garage round the corner, the owner's seventy and he'd sell for the land value. I'd fit it out with whatever the robot makers are selling by 2031. It's a gamble, but sitting still is a bigger one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Owning the business that owns the robots, but who'd be working there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer people, honestly, and I don't love that. I'd want to keep the ones who can manage the machines and talk to customers. I'd feel bad about the rest, but it's my money on the line, and that's how markets work.

say: Mechanics have a **head start** because robots come later, so use it.
He'd post **what he's doing** about it rather than panic online.
think: His **diagnosis skill** loses value in 2028 when AI does it better.
The only safe place is **owning the business** that owns the robots.
do: Offer Phil his **savings and project cars** for a share of Kenyon Motors.
Push the garage to be **first in the city** with new AI systems.
Propose at Christmas with a **cheaper ring** and put the rest into the business.
S2.quote: The only safe place is owning the business that owns the robots, not being the man they replace.
fieldNote: He answers a fast shock by **buying in**, not by retreating.
He admits a robot garage would employ **fewer people**, and is uneasy about it.
His backup is buying a retiring owner's **garage for land value**.

steps.text: Offer savings and two project cars for a share of Kenyon Motors
Make Kenyon Motors the first garage in the city on new AI systems
Buy a cheaper engagement ring and put the difference into the garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a proper business plan's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the picture where the people who get stuck in early do best. At church I'd say the same thing I'd say anywhere: look after your own and don't wait for someone to rescue you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years to AGI and eight to robots is a good window for someone like me. I'd be 35 when the robots come, with a share of a garage and a few years of running AI systems behind me. The risk is buying into a garage just before robots make garages cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd agree a deal with Phil to buy him out in stages over five years. I'd cut the car flips back to two a year so I can learn the management side properly. And I'd start a robotics maintenance course online this year, so I know what I'm buying when the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, alert way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is buying just before garages get cheap. How would you handle that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the garage's name and customer list, not the building. Rent the bricks, own the name. If robots make premises worthless, I haven't sunk everything into a building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth think of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd tell me to slow down, she always does. She's the careful one, which is good for me. We'd agree that the house deposit stays separate from anything I put into the garage.

say: People who **get stuck in early** do best in this one.
Look after your own and **don't wait** to be rescued.
think: Five years to AGI and eight to robots is a **good window** for him.
The danger is buying in **just before** robots make garages cheap.
do: Agree to **buy Phil out** in stages over five years.
Cut flips to **two a year** to learn the management side.
Start an online **robotics maintenance** course this year.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in an alert, energised way.
S3.quote: I'd buy the garage's name and customer list, not the building.
fieldNote: He thinks like an **investor**: buy the name, rent the bricks.
His girlfriend Ruth is the **careful one**, and they ring-fence the house deposit.
His traditional streak shows in **self-reliance**: don't wait to be rescued.

steps.text: Buy Phil Kenyon out of the garage in stages over five years
Start an online robotics maintenance course this year
Keep the house deposit separate from money put into the garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone not to be ready, but I'd say it kindly to the parents at football. At work I'd tell Phil we've got a decade to become the best garage in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the one I'm happiest with. By 2036 I could own Kenyon Motors outright, and by 2039 I'd be choosing which robots to buy rather than worrying about being replaced by one. I'd be 40, settled, maybe with kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd propose at Christmas as planned and start saving for a wedding and a house. I'd agree a slow buy-in with Phil over ten years. I'd keep the flips going at four a year, because that's my safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is a lot of time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about, even in this calmer picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kids I coach at football are eleven, so in ten years they're starting work just as the robots arrive. I'd tell the parents to get them a trade and get them good with these tools, both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell them exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the boys and girls who can fix things and run the machines doing the fixing will always find work. I'd say university is fine, but a trade plus the tools is worth more. And I'd offer the keen ones a Saturday job at the garage when they're sixteen.

say: There's **no excuse** not to be ready, said kindly to football parents.
Kenyon Motors has a decade to become **the best garage** in the city.
think: By 2036 he could **own Kenyon Motors** outright.
By 2039 he'd be **choosing robots** to buy rather than fearing replacement.
do: Propose at **Christmas** and start saving for a wedding and house.
Agree a **slow buy-in** with Phil over ten years.
Keep **four flips a year** as a safety net.
feel: **Calm**, because ten years is a lot of time to get ready.
S4.quote: The kids I coach at football are eleven, so in ten years they're starting work just as the robots arrive.
fieldNote: With a decade he moves from worker to **owner** with little fear.
His worry turns to the **eleven-year-olds** he coaches, who start work as robots arrive.
He'd offer keen kids **Saturday jobs** at the garage, passing the trade on.

steps.text: Propose to Ruth at Christmas and start a wedding and house fund
Agree a ten-year buy-in of Kenyon Motors with Phil
Keep flipping four auction cars a year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to buy in before the AI takes the diagnosis work. What would help is banks lending to small garages to buy the new kit, so it's not just the big chains that own the robots. Apart from that, keep the government out of it, they'd only slow things down.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who ends up owning all this. If the big chains own every robot, a mechanic like me never gets a garage of his own. I'd rather the robots were owned by ten thousand small garages than three big chains.

headlineQuote: I'd rather the robots were owned by ten thousand small garages than three big chains.
portrait: Marco is a 27-year-old mechanic at **Kenyon Motors** who set up its AI booking system.
He flips **auction cars** on the side and wants to own a garage one day.
He's traditional and self-reliant: church, coaching **under-twelves football**, and little faith in government help.
In the fast AGI picture he answers fear by **buying in** to the business that will own the robots.
With more warning he plans a **slow buy-out** of his boss and stays calm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to buy into a garage before AI takes diagnosis.
whatWouldHelp: **Bank loans** for small garages to buy new kit, so chains don't own every robot.
Otherwise keeping the **government out** of it.
